### parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d

Identification of Young's modulus of an elliptic plate with Dirichlet and Neumann
boundaries, with the gradient computed by forward-mode automatic differentiation
(f-AD). This is the third of three benchmarks for gradient-based optimization in
linear elastic solid mechanics. Unlike the periodic benchmarks
(`periodicPlateOptiAD2d`, `periodicPlateOptiParam2d` and `periodicPlateOpti2d`), where
the control acts on the body force, the control here is a material parameter, and the
curved boundaries reduce the primal scheme to first order.

The benchmark and its results are described in
[@grafenBenchmarkCasesGradientbased2026].

#### Setup

The numerical domain is $\Omega = [0, 1.5]^2$, discretized by $N_x + 1$ lattice nodes
per Cartesian direction. The PDE constraint is enforced on the elliptic plate
$\Omega^E$ of [@boolakee:23b], an outer ellipse from which two inner ellipses are
removed, with the geometric parameters

| Ellipse | $a_i^2$ | $b_i^2$ | $x_i$ | $y_i$ | $\phi_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0.48L^2$ | $0.3L^2$ | $0.750L$ | $0.750L$ | $-\pi/9$ |
| 2 | $0.010L^2$ | $0.018L^2$ | $0.950L$ | $0.600L$ | $0$ |
| 3 | $0.035L^2$ | $0.010L^2$ | $0.500L$ | $0.900L$ | $0$ |

for the characteristic length $L = 1$. The outer contour is a traction (Neumann)
boundary, the two inner contours are displacement (Dirichlet) boundaries, which is the
combined configuration of
`structuralmechanics/linearElasticity/quasistationary/combinedEllipse` and follows the
OpenLB implementation of [@kaiser:25].

![The elliptic plate with its boundary conditions. The outer contour carries the traction (Neumann) condition, the two inner contours the prescribed displacement (Dirichlet) condition. Reproduced from [@grafenBenchmarkCasesGradientbased2026].](/examples/optimization/parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d/doc/fig/ellipse_domain.png){#fig-ellipse-domain width="60%"}

Following [@boolakee:23b] the manufactured steady-state displacement is

$$
\symbf{u}^*(\symbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix}
  \delta_1 \sin(2\pi x_1 x_2) \\
  \delta_2 \cos(2\pi x_2)(1 + x_1^2)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \delta_1 = 9 \cdot 10^{-4}, \quad \delta_2 = 7 \cdot 10^{-4},
$$

with the associated stress following from the constitutive relation. The body force,
the Dirichlet data and the traction are evaluated for the reference material
$E^* = 0.1$ and $\nu = 0.7$. The initial displacement is $\symbf{u}(\symbf{x}, t=0) = \symbf{0}$.

#### Inverse problem

Young's modulus is the control. To keep it physically admissible without a constrained
optimizer, it is substituted as

$$
E = \alpha^2 \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}, \qquad \alpha \in \mathbb{R},
$$

so the optimizer works on an unconstrained scalar and $E > 0$ holds by construction.
The reference control is $\alpha^* = \sqrt{E^*}$. The map $\alpha \mapsto \alpha^2$ has
the two minimizers $\pm\alpha^*$, so the recovered control is determined only up to its
sign and the error is reported for $|\alpha|$. The objective is evaluated on the
discretized elliptic domain $\Omega^E_{\Delta x}$.

Because the control enters through the relaxation frequencies of the scheme, the state
depends nonlinearly on $\alpha$ — in contrast to the periodic benchmarks, where the
scheme is linear in the control.

##### Loads must not follow the control

The boundary conditions and the body force are data of the inverse problem and are held
fixed throughout the optimization; only their representation in lattice units depends
on the control. In particular the traction $\symbf{T} = \symbf{\sigma}^*\symbf{n}$ has to be
evaluated with the reference moduli $\mu(E^*)$ and $K(E^*)$. If it were evaluated with
the control of the current optimization step, the dependence on $E$ would cancel on
$\partial\Omega_N$ and the Neumann boundary would carry no information about the
material.

This is why the outer contour uses
`StationaryLinearElasticityMRTNeumannValidationFixedMaterial` instead of the
`StationaryLinearElasticityMRTNeumannValidation` of the forward example
`combinedEllipse`. It reads the moduli of the manufactured traction from the dedicated
parameters `structuralmechanics::REFERENCE_LAME_MU` and
`structuralmechanics::REFERENCE_BULK_MODULUS`, set to the lattice moduli of a second
`StationaryMRTUnitConverter` built at the target modulus, while
`structuralmechanics::LAME_MU` and `BULK_MODULUS` carry the lattice moduli of the
simulated (controlled) material. Both variants share the implementation
`TractionFromManufacturedStress<MU, BULK>` and differ only in the two parameters they
read.

All four parameters hold lattice moduli. The strain of the manufactured displacement is
dimensionless, so a stress built from lattice moduli is already in lattice units. The
lattice value of the target moduli depends on the conversion factor
$\kappa \Delta x^2 / \Delta t$ of the simulation, and without `FIXED_TIME_STEP` the
time step follows the control. `targetConverter` therefore shares $\Delta x$ and
$\Delta t$ with the simulated lattice, and `prepareLattice` sets both parameters anew in
every optimization step. The forward variant, in contrast, evaluates the traction for
the simulated material in either time-step mode.

The same applies to the body force. $\symbf{F}^*$ follows from inserting the
manufactured displacement into the steady Navier--Cauchy equation, so it is
proportional to the moduli it is evaluated with. It is a load, fixed by the problem,
and must therefore also be built at $E^*$. `setInitialValues` does this explicitly:

```cpp
ForceField2D<T> force(targetConverter.getLameMu(),
                      targetConverter.getLameLambda(),
                      converter.getConversionFactorSolidForce());
fields::set<descriptors::FORCE>(lattice, geometry.getMaterialIndicator({1}), force);
```

Note the split between the two converters. The two moduli come from
`targetConverter`, built at `TARGET_YOUNGS_MODULUS`, because they fix the physical
load; the conversion factor comes from the controlled `converter`, because only the
*representation* of that load in lattice units may follow the control. Building the
force with the controlled moduli instead would make the applied load scale with $E$
together with the stiffness it is probing, and the identification would lose most of
its sensitivity to the control.

#### Implementation

`case.h` defines `MyCase` as a `Case<names::NavierCauchy, Lattice<double, D2Q8<>>>`,
derives `MyADfCase = MyCase::exchange_value_t<ADf>` and combines them in an
`OptiCaseADf<Controlled, MyCase, Derivatives, MyADfCase, Reference, MyCase>`. With a
one-dimensional control, a single tangent direction suffices and f-AD is the efficient
choice. `analyticalSolution.h` holds the manufactured fields.

#### Files

```
parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d/
├── parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d.cpp  main(): default parameters, optimizer settings, run
├── case.h                                     Case and OptiCase types, geometry, lattice, objective
├── analyticalSolution.h                       ellipse level sets, manufactured displacement, stress and force
├── forward_study.xml                          case file: primal grid convergence study
└── Makefile
```

Every parameter set in the `.cpp` can be overridden on the command line
(`--RESOLUTION 80`) or collected in a case file passed with `--case-file`. The
precedence is `set<>()` < case file < command line, so a case file pins what
belongs to a study while the command line varies the rest.

`forward_study.xml` turns the example into the primal grid convergence study:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `FORWARD_ONLY 1` | solve the primal problem once at the target modulus $E^* = 0.1$ and write the error CSVs instead of optimizing |
| `FIXED_TIME_STEP 1` | pin $\Delta t$ to the value belonging to the target modulus instead of letting it follow the control |
| `PHYS_MAX_T 90` | with $\Delta x = 1.5/N_x$, a fixed budget of $40 N_x^2$ steps |
| `CONVERGENCE_PRECISION 0` | disables the steady-state stopping rule, so every resolution runs the same budget |
| `LATTICE_LOG_ITER_T 100000000` | silences the per-step log |

Disabling the stopping rule is what makes the study measure the discretization
error alone. With a tolerance active the run stops at a point that depends on the
resolution, and on the summation order of the lattice-wide average that the
convergence check watches — which is not the same on CPU and GPU.

`FIXED_TIME_STEP` matters for the inverse problem too, and is the reason the
resolution study passes it on the command line. The relaxation frequencies follow
the control, so with a control-dependent $\Delta t$ the iteration budget itself
would change from one optimization step to the next.

#### Parameters

All of the following are set in `parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d.cpp` and can
be overridden from a case file or the command line. `INITIAL_CONTROL` is a scalar
here, not a vector, because the control is the single modulus.

##### Geometry and discretization

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RESOLUTION` | int | `40` | nodes per Cartesian direction, $N_x$; the elliptic domain is carved out of the square lattice |
| `DOMAIN_EXTENT` | double[2] | `{1.5, 1.5}` | physical size of the square that contains the plate |
| `PHYS_CHAR_LENGTH` | double | `1.0` | characteristic length $L$ of the ellipse parameters |
| `PHYS_DELTA_X` | double | derived | $\Delta x =$ `DOMAIN_EXTENT[0] / RESOLUTION` |
| `ORIGIN` | double[2] | derived | lower-left corner, set to $(\Delta x, \Delta x)$ so the boundary does not land on the lattice edge |
| `LATTICE_MAX_T` | size_t | derived | step cap, computed once as `PHYS_MAX_T`$/\Delta x^2$ |
| `PHYS_CHAR_DISPLACEMENT` | double | derived | displacement scale of the converter, set to $\Delta x$ |

$\Delta t$ is deliberately absent from this list: it depends on the control and is
set in `prepareLattice`. The iteration budget must not move with it, which is why
`LATTICE_MAX_T` is derived once from $\Delta x^2$ rather than from $\Delta t$.

##### Material and control target

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOLID_CASE` | string | `"continua"` | dimensional reduction of the constitutive law; accepts `continua`, `planeStress`, `planeStrain` and `standard` |
| `YOUNGS_MODULUS` | double | `0.15` | $E$ the simulation starts from; it is the control and changes every optimization step |
| `TARGET_YOUNGS_MODULUS` | double | `0.1` | $E^*$, the modulus the loads and the target displacement were generated with |
| `POISSON_RATIO` | double | `0.7` | $\nu$, held fixed |
| `PHYS_DENSITY` | double | `1.0` | $\rho$ |
| `DAMPING_FACTOR` | double | `1.0` | $\kappa$ of the damped pseudo-time scheme; also sets the stress conversion factor |

`TARGET_YOUNGS_MODULUS` is what builds the second unit converter behind
`REFERENCE_LAME_MU` and `REFERENCE_BULK_MODULUS`, so changing it moves the
loads as well as the answer.

##### Pseudo-time stepping and convergence

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PHYS_MAX_T` | double | `60` | pseudo-time budget; converted once into `LATTICE_MAX_T`. The benchmark's forward study uses `90`, giving $40 N_x^2$ steps |
| `CONVERGENCE_PRECISION` | double | `1e-7` | relative tolerance of the steady-state check; `0` disables the check and runs the full budget. The benchmark study uses `1e-6` |
| `CONV_ITER` | double | `10` | window length of the `ValueTracer` that watches the monitored value |
| `CONV_VALUE` | double | `1` | slot the case writes the monitored value into; not a user knob |
| `CONVERGED` | bool | `false` | slot recording whether the last solve met the tolerance; not a user knob |
| `FIXED_TIME_STEP` | bool | `false` | `true` pins $\Delta t$ to the value belonging to the target modulus instead of letting it follow the control |

##### Inverse problem

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INITIAL_CONTROL` | double | `0.15` | given as $E^{(0)}$, not as $\alpha^{(0)}$; the case takes the root internally, so the optimizer starts at $\alpha^{(0)} = \sqrt{E^{(0)}}$ |
| `ANALYTICAL_REFERENCE` | bool | `true` | `true` compares against the sampled manufactured displacement, `false` against a reference obtained from a simulation |
| `FORWARD_ONLY` | bool | `false` | `true` solves the primal problem once at $E^*$ and writes the error CSVs, skipping the optimization entirely |

##### Output

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OPTI_VTK_ENABLED` | bool | `true` | write VTK fields during the optimization; note the name differs from the `VTK_ENABLED` of the periodic cases |
| `LATTICE_VTK_ITER_T` | int | `1000` | pseudo-time steps between VTK writes |
| `LATTICE_LOG_ITER_T` | int | `100` | pseudo-time steps between console log lines; a very large value silences the log |

##### Optimizer

Held in a separate `OptimizerParametersD` in `main()` rather than in the case
parameters, and namespaced by optimizer component.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `optimizer::EPS` | double | `1e-10` | termination tolerance on the gradient norm |
| `optimizer::MAX_OPTIMIZATION_STEPS` | int | `50` | cap on the number of optimization steps |
| `optimizer::VERBOSE` | bool | `true` | per-step optimizer log |
| `linesearch::MAX_STEP_ATTEMPTS` | int | `100` | cap on line-search refinements within one step |

#### Different modes of running the case

**Inverse problem**:
The default mode, selected by passing no case file, so that `FORWARD_ONLY` is
`false` and the f-AD optimization loop runs. The defaults solve $N_x = 40$ starting
from $E^{(0)} = 0.15$ towards $E^* = 0.1$. The resolution study uses the looser
steady-state tolerance $10^{-6}$ and a time step that does not follow the control:

```sh
mpirun -np 4 ./parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d \
  --CONVERGENCE_PRECISION 1e-6 --RESOLUTION 40 --FIXED_TIME_STEP 1
```

repeated over $N_x \in \{40, 80, 120, 160\}$, with `--INITIAL_CONTROL 0.07` (or
`0.19`) for the initial-value study. The optimization history is written to
`tmp/gnuplotData/data/optiLog.dat`.

**Forward grid convergence study**:
Selected by `forward_study.xml`, which solves the primal problem once at the target
modulus with the stopping rule disabled, for a fixed budget of $40 N_x^2$ steps:

```sh
./parameterIdentificationEllipseCombo2d --case-file forward_study.xml --RESOLUTION 64
```

Each run appends one row `N,L2,LInf` to `tmp/gnuplotData/data/disp_err.csv` and
`stress_err.csv`, so all resolutions have to run in the same directory for the
study to collect.

#### Results

The results of this benchmark are reported and discussed in
[@grafenBenchmarkCasesGradientbased2026]: the order of convergence of the primal
problem on the curved boundaries, the evolution of the objective, of the gradient
magnitude and of the relative control error over the resolutions, and the
influence of the initial modulus on the optimization.
